patterns.signal: Prices, balances or tax are stored as `float`/`double` and totals are off by a cent
patterns.use: Integer minor units or a decimal type
patterns.why: Store integer cents (or a decimal type) so 0.1 is exact and sums are exact. Decide rounding rules explicitly at the points where division or tax happens.

patterns.signal: A computed float is compared with `==` and the check fails intermittently
patterns.why: Compare `abs(a - b) <= eps`, with a relative term for large magnitudes. Floats are deterministic approximations; exact equality only holds for values that are exactly representable.

patterns.signal: 64-bit database IDs reach a JavaScript client as JSON numbers and two records show the same ID
patterns.why: JS numbers are doubles with 53 bits of precision, so larger integers silently round. Send IDs as strings (or parse to `BigInt`) and never do arithmetic on them.

patterns.signal: Text such as `JosÃ©` appears after a round trip through a file, socket or database
patterns.why: Mojibake means bytes were decoded with the wrong encoding. Decode bytes to text once on input and encode once on output, always naming the encoding instead of trusting a platform default.

patterns.signal: A length limit, truncation or cursor move breaks on accented names or emoji
patterns.use: Count the right unit of length
patterns.why: Bytes, code points and grapheme clusters differ. Use bytes for storage limits, graphemes for what users see, and never slice text at a byte offset that may split a multibyte character.

patterns.signal: A counter, millisecond tick or Unix timestamp is held in a signed 32-bit integer
patterns.why: 32-bit ms counters wrap after about 24.8 days and 32-bit timestamps in 2038. Use 64-bit types, and checked arithmetic where wrap would be silent, at the cost of 4 extra bytes per value.

patterns.signal: Objects far from the world origin jitter, and physics or camera get less precise the further the player travels
patterns.why: Float32 spacing grows with magnitude, so precision drops far from zero. Periodically shift the world back to the origin, or keep 64-bit positions and render camera-relative.

patterns.signal: Each item carries a dozen independent booleans that are tested, combined and stored together
patterns.why: Pack flags into one integer and test with `flags & MASK`: compact, cheap to copy, and many flags combine in one operation. Costs readability, so name every mask and cap the count at the integer width.

patterns.signal: A loop over `n` orders calls `customers.find(...)` or a linear search on another collection
patterns.why: Index the inner collection by key before the loop, turning O(n·m) into O(n + m). Costs O(m) memory; only worth it when the lookups repeat.

patterns.signal: A loop issues one database or HTTP call per item and latency grows with the number of rows
patterns.why: Fetch everything in one `WHERE id IN (...)` or a join, then match in memory. One round trip replaces n, though very large batches may need chunking.

patterns.signal: A string is built with `s += piece` inside a loop over thousands of items
patterns.why: With immutable strings each `+=` can copy the whole string so far, giving O(n^2). Append to a list or string builder and join once for O(n) total.

patterns.signal: You must remove duplicates from a large list and keep the first-seen order
patterns.why: Scan once, skip items already in a hash set: O(n) expected time and O(n) extra memory. Items must be hashable and stable while in the set.

patterns.signal: You must dedupe or group a huge dataset, memory is tight or the output should be sorted anyway
patterns.why: After sorting, equal items are adjacent, so one pass finds duplicates or groups. O(n log n) instead of O(n), but works in place or externally and gives sorted output.

patterns.signal: You need the top 10 of millions of scores and the code sorts the whole list first
patterns.use: Partial selection with a size-k heap
patterns.why: A min-heap holding k items costs O(n log k) time and O(k) memory, and works on streams. A full sort costs O(n log n) and needs everything in memory.

patterns.signal: In a hot loop over about 20 small items, a hash map is slower than a plain array scan in the profiler
patterns.use: Linear scan over a contiguous array
patterns.why: At small n, constants and cache locality dominate Big-O; a contiguous scan avoids hashing and pointer chasing. Re-measure if n can grow into the thousands.

patterns.signal: Someone argues a call is O(1) or O(n log n) so it cannot be the cause of a slowdown
patterns.why: Big-O predicts growth, not absolute cost: an O(1) call can block on I/O for seconds. Use Big-O to rule out bad designs, then profile with realistic input sizes.

patterns.signal: You test `x in items` inside a loop and `items` is a list
patterns.why: Average O(1) membership instead of O(n), so an O(n·m) loop becomes O(n + m). Costs extra memory per entry and gives no ordering guarantee.

patterns.signal: Queries ask for keys in a range, the nearest key, or sorted iteration (orders between two dates)
patterns.use: Sorted array or balanced search tree
patterns.why: Both give O(log n) search and in-order range scans. A sorted array with binary search is compact and fastest if built once; use a balanced tree when inserts and deletes are frequent.

patterns.signal: Code repeatedly asks for the smallest or highest-priority item while items keep arriving (jobs, timers)
patterns.why: O(log n) push and pop-min, O(1) peek. A heap is not sorted, so it cannot do range queries or fast arbitrary search; use a balanced tree when you need those.

patterns.signal: Work items are processed in arrival order and the code uses `list.pop(0)` or `array.shift()`
patterns.why: `pop(0)` shifts every remaining element, so draining n items is O(n^2). A deque or ring buffer gives O(1) at both ends; bound its size if producers can outrun consumers.

patterns.signal: The requirement says undo, nested scopes, matching brackets or return to the previous state
patterns.why: Last-in-first-out matches nesting: push on open or action, pop on close or undo, both O(1). For redo, keep a second stack and clear it on each new action.

patterns.signal: Autocomplete, longest-prefix match or 'all words starting with ...' over a large vocabulary
patterns.why: Lookup costs O(length of key) regardless of vocabulary size, and all completions sit under one node. Uses much more memory than a hash set; a sorted array with binary search on prefixes is a compact alternative.

patterns.signal: Items are merged into groups over time and you ask 'are A and B connected?' (islands, clusters, Kruskal)
patterns.why: With path compression and union by rank, union and find are effectively O(1) amortized. It cannot split groups or list a path; use graph search for those.

patterns.signal: Entities link to a handful of others (dependencies, roads, friends) and there are tens of thousands of them
patterns.why: O(V + E) memory and fast neighbour iteration for sparse graphs. Use an adjacency matrix only when the graph is small or dense and you need O(1) 'is there an edge' checks.

patterns.signal: A cache must hold at most N entries and evict the least recently used one in O(1)
patterns.why: The map finds a node in O(1); the list keeps recency order so moving to front and evicting the tail are O(1). Many languages ship this as an ordered dictionary.

patterns.signal: A huge grid or matrix is mostly empty and the dense array eats memory (chunk maps, sparse tiles)
patterns.why: Store only occupied cells in a hash map keyed by `(x, y)`: memory scales with content, not area. Iteration is unordered and each access hashes, so switch back to dense arrays when most cells are filled.

patterns.signal: You track membership for small dense integer IDs and intersect or union large sets often (layers, visited flags)
patterns.why: One bit per possible ID; intersection and union run 64 IDs per machine word. Memory scales with the largest ID, not the count, so it is wasteful when IDs are sparse.

patterns.signal: A linked structure may loop back on itself and you must detect the cycle without extra memory
patterns.why: Advance one pointer by 1 and another by 2; they meet if and only if there is a cycle. O(n) time and O(1) memory; a visited hash set is simpler but costs O(n) memory.

patterns.signal: The data is sorted (or monotonic) and you search for a value, the first item >= x, or an insertion point
patterns.why: O(log n) instead of O(n). Only correct if the data really is sorted by the same key; sorting first costs O(n log n), which pays off only for repeated queries.

patterns.signal: Sorted array, and the question asks for a pair or triple with a target sum, or to merge or dedupe in place
patterns.why: Move a left and a right index inward based on the comparison: O(n) time, O(1) memory. Relies on sorted order; on unsorted input use a hash set of complements.

patterns.signal: Longest or shortest contiguous subarray or substring that satisfies a constraint (at most k distinct, sum >= s)
patterns.why: Grow the right edge, shrink the left while the window is invalid: O(n) instead of O(n^2). Needs the constraint to be monotonic in window size; negative numbers can break sum windows.

patterns.signal: Many queries ask for the sum of `a[i..j]` on an array that rarely changes
patterns.why: Precompute `P[k] = a[0] + ... + a[k-1]` once in O(n); each query is `P[j+1] - P[i]` in O(1). Updates cost O(n), so use a Fenwick or segment tree when values change often.

patterns.signal: For each element, find the next greater or smaller element, or how far a span extends (stock span, histogram)
patterns.why: Keep a stack of indices with increasing or decreasing values; each index is pushed and popped once, so O(n) total instead of O(n^2) nested scans.

patterns.signal: Fewest hops or moves between two states where every edge costs the same (social graph, grid maze)
patterns.why: Exploring level by level from a queue finds a fewest-edge path in O(V + E). Mark nodes visited when enqueued; with unequal edge weights BFS is no longer correct.

patterns.signal: Shortest path where edges have different non-negative costs (travel times, movement costs)
patterns.why: A min-heap of tentative distances gives O((V + E) log V). Fails with negative weights (use Bellman-Ford); add an admissible heuristic to get A* for single-target queries.

patterns.signal: Tasks, packages or build steps must run after the things they depend on
patterns.why: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly takes nodes with no remaining prerequisites, O(V + E). If nodes are left over, the graph has a cycle, which is also how you report circular dependencies.

patterns.signal: The requirement says all combinations, permutations or placements that satisfy constraints (sudoku, seating)
patterns.why: Build a candidate step by step and undo on a dead end. Worst case stays exponential, so prune early on violated constraints and switch to DP if subproblems repeat.

patterns.signal: A recursive solution recomputes the same arguments many times and slows explosively as input grows
patterns.why: Define the state, recurrence and base cases, then memoize or fill a table, so each subproblem is solved once. Needs optimal substructure; table memory can dominate for large state spaces.

patterns.signal: Taking the best-looking option at each step seems to work (earliest finish time, largest coin)
patterns.why: Greedy is fast and simple but only correct with the greedy-choice property, as in interval scheduling by earliest finish. Coins {1, 3, 4} for 6 show it failing; check against brute force on small inputs.

patterns.signal: The question asks to minimise the maximum (or maximise the minimum): smallest capacity, fewest days, largest gap
patterns.why: If 'can we do it with limit X?' is monotonic in X, binary search X and run a cheap feasibility check each time: O(log range · check). Fails if feasibility is not monotonic.

patterns.signal: A function has a mutable default such as `def f(x, acc=[])` and results accumulate across calls
patterns.why: The default object is created once and shared by every call. Default to `None` and create a fresh list inside; do the same for dicts, sets and any mutable object.

patterns.signal: You copied a list or object, changed a nested field, and the original changed too
patterns.use: Deep copy or immutable nested data
patterns.why: A shallow copy duplicates only the outer container; nested objects are still shared. Deep copy when you must mutate, or keep nested data immutable so sharing is safe and cheap.

patterns.signal: Memory climbs steadily for days and a static map or cache is only ever added to
patterns.why: The GC cannot free what stays reachable. Cap entries and evict by LRU or TTL, or key by weak references when entries should die with their owner. Unbounded growth is a leak by design.

patterns.signal: Destroyed screens, scenes or objects stay in a heap snapshot, retained by event handlers or callbacks
patterns.why: A publisher's listener list keeps every subscriber reachable. Pair every subscribe with an unsubscribe in the matching teardown hook, or hold a disposable token that removes the handler.

patterns.signal: A lookup by an object key fails after one of the key object's fields was changed
patterns.why: The entry sits in the bucket for its old hash, so changed keys become unfindable. Use immutable keys (tuples, records, IDs) and never mutate an object while it is a key.

patterns.signal: Recursion that is logically correct crashes with a stack overflow on very deep or long inputs
patterns.why: Each call costs a stack frame and the call stack is small. An explicit heap-allocated stack or loop handles depth bounded only by memory; raising the recursion limit just moves the crash.

patterns.signal: The profiler shows periodic GC spikes while many short-lived objects (bullets, buffers, messages) are created per second
patterns.why: Reusing pre-allocated objects keeps allocation off the hot path and GC quiet. Costs reset bookkeeping and memory held at peak size; stale state in reused objects is the classic bug.

patterns.signal: A benchmark on a JIT runtime shows the first thousand calls far slower than later ones
patterns.why: JIT code starts interpreted and is compiled once it is hot. Discard warm-up iterations and use a benchmark harness; but report cold-start time separately if users actually pay it.

patterns.signal: Code reads shared state, checks it (`stock > 0`), then writes; overselling or double-booking shows up rarely
patterns.why: Make check and write one operation: `UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0`, compare-and-swap, or a unique constraint. Check-then-act is a race whatever the language.

patterns.signal: Several threads increment a shared counter or flag and the total comes out too low
patterns.why: An atomic increment or CAS is lock-free and cheap for one word. Once an invariant spans several fields, atomics compose badly; switch to a lock around the whole update.

patterns.signal: An invariant spans several fields or objects (balance plus ledger entry) touched by multiple threads
patterns.why: One lock guarding every read and write of the related fields keeps them consistent. Locks serialise work and can deadlock, so keep the critical section short and never call unknown code inside.

patterns.signal: Two threads hang forever, each holding one lock and waiting for the other's (`accounts[1]`, `accounts[2]`)
patterns.why: Always acquire locks in one agreed order, for example by account id, so a wait cycle cannot form. Lock timeouts only detect deadlock; ordering prevents it.

patterns.signal: A lock is held across a network call, disk read or `await`, and throughput collapses under load
patterns.why: Do the slow I/O outside the lock, then lock only to read or apply the result, revalidating if needed. Every millisecond inside the lock serialises all waiting threads.

patterns.signal: One part produces work (requests, log lines, chunks) faster or slower than another part consumes it
patterns.why: A thread-safe queue decouples the two sides and gives each worker data it owns. Bound it so a fast producer blocks or sheds load instead of exhausting memory.

patterns.signal: Read-mostly configuration or lookup data is shared by many threads and someone proposes a lock on every read
patterns.why: Readers use an immutable object with no locks; a writer builds a new copy and publishes it with one atomic reference swap. Costs a full copy per update, so it suits rare writes.

patterns.signal: Independent I/O calls are awaited one after another, so latency is their sum
patterns.why: Start them together and join with `Promise.all` or a task group, so latency becomes the slowest one. Cap concurrency for large fan-outs and decide how one failure cancels the rest.

patterns.signal: One CPU-heavy request (compression, image resize, `gzipSync`) freezes an async server for every user
patterns.use: Offload CPU work to a worker pool
patterns.why: The event loop is one thread, so CPU-bound work blocks all other tasks. Use async APIs or worker threads or processes; async alone speeds up waiting, not computing.
